name: Upper limb bones (right)
description: Right pectoral girdle, arm and forearm: clavicle, scapula, humerus, radius and ulna, with the hand for context.

Structures marked "merged" are the union of several BodyParts3D meshes (e.g. the parts of one muscle); structures with a "component" take one connected part of a BodyParts3D mesh, chosen by position.

groups.label: Upper limb
groups.tip: Work outwards from the trunk: collarbone and shoulder blade, then the humerus, then the radius and ulna, and finally the hand.

groups.label: Pectoral (shoulder) girdle
groups.tip: The collarbone and shoulder blade join your trunk at just one small joint by the breastbone. Muscles hold the rest, which is why your shoulder moves so freely.

groups.label: Arm
groups.tip: In anatomy, the arm is only the part between shoulder and elbow. So it has just one bone, the humerus.

groups.label: Forearm
groups.tip: Radius by the thumb, ulna by the little finger. Turn your palm down and the radius crosses over the ulna, which stays still.

groups.label: Hand (context)
groups.tip: Wrist bones, top row from thumb to pinky, then the bottom row back again: So Long To Pinky, Here Comes The Thumb.

content.origin: From the Latin for little key. Its gentle S-shaped curve looks like an old-fashioned key.
content.location: It runs across the top of your chest, just under the skin, from the breastbone out to the point of your shoulder.
content.description: A long bone shaped like a gentle S. You can feel it along its whole length.
content.function: It works like a strut, holding your shoulder out from your body so your arm can swing freely. It is the only bone that links your arm to your trunk.
content.mnemonic: Clavicle means little key. Picture an S-shaped key that locks your shoulder to your chest.
content.clinical: It is one of the most often broken bones, usually in its middle, from a fall on the shoulder or an outstretched hand. The shoulder then droops forward and down.
content.hint: Find the S-shaped bone running across the top of the chest from the breastbone to the point of the shoulder.

questions.text: Which bone is the only bony link between your arm and your trunk?
questions.explanation: The clavicle joins the breastbone at the sternoclavicular joint. The shoulder blade is held on only by muscles.

questions.text: Where does the clavicle most often break?
questions.explanation: Most clavicle breaks happen in the middle third of the bone.

content.origin: From the Latin for shoulder blade. It really does look like a flat blade.
content.location: It lies flat on your upper back over the ribs, one on each side of the spine.
content.description: A flat triangle of bone. A ridge crosses its back and ends at the point of your shoulder, and at the outer corner is a shallow socket for the arm.
content.function: Its shallow socket holds the top of the arm bone to form the shoulder joint. It anchors many muscles, including the rotator cuff, and glides over your ribs to give your arm more reach.
content.mnemonic: Remember four landmarks as a ridge, a roof, a hook and a socket. They are the spine, acromion, coracoid and glenoid.
content.clinical: If the long thoracic nerve is damaged, the inner edge of the blade sticks out like a wing. It shows best when the person pushes against a wall.
content.hint: Find the flat triangle on the upper back with a ridge across it, a hook at the front and a shallow socket for the arm.

questions.text: The top of the humerus fits into which part of the scapula?
questions.explanation: The glenoid cavity is the shallow socket of the shoulder joint. The ball at the top of the humerus sits in it.

questions.text: A winged scapula is usually caused by injury to which nerve?
questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve powers serratus anterior, the muscle that holds the shoulder blade flat against the ribs.

content.origin: From the Latin word for shoulder or upper arm.
content.location: It is the only bone in your upper arm, running from the shoulder blade down to the two forearm bones at the elbow.
content.description: A long bone with a smooth ball at the top. At the elbow it has a pulley, the trochlea, for the ulna and a round knob, the capitulum, for the radius.
content.function: It forms the shoulder joint above and the elbow joint below. It is the lever for most arm movements and anchors big muscles like the deltoid.
content.mnemonic: Nerves at risk, top to bottom, spell A R U. Axillary at the neck, Radial along the shaft, Ulnar behind the elbow.
content.clinical: A break through its shaft can hurt the radial nerve, so the wrist flops down, called wrist drop. The ulnar nerve behind the elbow is your tingly funny bone.
content.hint: Find the single long bone of the upper arm, with a ball at the shoulder and a pulley shape at the elbow.

questions.text: A break along the shaft of the humerus can damage the radial nerve. What problem can this cause?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve runs in a groove along the humerus and powers the muscles that lift the wrist. Injury makes the wrist flop down.

questions.text: Which part of the lower humerus meets the ulna?
questions.explanation: The pulley-shaped trochlea fits into the notch of the ulna. The rounded capitulum meets the radius instead.

content.origin: From the Latin for the spoke of a wheel. It turns around the ulna like a spoke.
content.location: It is the forearm bone on your thumb side, running from the elbow to the wrist beside the ulna.
content.description: A long bone, slim at the elbow and wide at the wrist. Its top is a flat disc, and just below it is a bump where the biceps pulls.
content.function: Its disc-shaped head spins against the humerus as it rolls around the ulna, turning your palm up and down. Its wide lower end forms most of the wrist joint.
content.mnemonic: Radius by the thumb. Give a thumbs up for the radius.
content.clinical: Falling on an outstretched hand often breaks its wrist end, a Colles fracture. In young children, a sudden tug on the arm can slip its head out of place, called pulled elbow.
content.hint: Find the forearm bone on the thumb side, with a disc-shaped top at the elbow and a wide lower end at the wrist.

questions.text: Which movement depends on the radius rolling around the ulna?
options: Turning the palm up and down
questions.explanation: Turning a key or a doorknob works because the radius rolls around the ulna, turning your palm up and down.

questions.text: The head of the radius meets which part of the humerus?
questions.explanation: The capitulum is the round knob on the outer side of the lower humerus. The disc-shaped head of the radius spins against it.

content.origin: From the Latin word for elbow or forearm. Its top end is the point of your elbow.
content.location: It is the forearm bone on your little-finger side, running from the elbow to the wrist beside the radius.
content.description: A long bone, big at the elbow and small at the wrist. Its top end has a deep C-shaped notch, with the olecranon, the point of your elbow, behind it.
content.function: Its C-shaped notch grips the humerus to make the elbow's main hinge. Triceps pulls on the olecranon to straighten your arm, and the radius turns around this steady bone.
content.mnemonic: Ulna goes with the little finger. The olecranon is the elbow you lean on at the table.
content.clinical: Landing on the point of the elbow can break the olecranon. A Monteggia fracture is a break of the ulna with the top of the radius knocked out of place.
content.hint: Find the forearm bone on the little-finger side, whose top end forms the bony point of the elbow.

questions.text: The olecranon, the bony point of the elbow, belongs to which bone?
questions.explanation: The olecranon is the top end of the ulna. It is the part you lean on when you rest your elbows on a table.

questions.text: Which muscle attaches to the olecranon of the ulna?
questions.explanation: Triceps brachii, on the back of your arm, pulls on the olecranon to straighten the elbow.

names.preferred: Bones of the hand (carpals and metacarpals)

content.origin: From the Greek karpos, meaning wrist. Meta means beyond, so the metacarpals lie beyond the wrist.
content.location: It sits just past the lower ends of the radius and ulna. It is shown here only to complete the arm.
content.description: Eight small wrist bones in two rows of four, plus five palm bones, one for each finger. The finger bones are not included in this model.
content.function: The wrist bones meet the radius and give your hand a flexible base. The palm bones form the frame of your palm.
content.mnemonic: Wrist bones, top row from thumb to pinky, then the bottom row back again: So Long To Pinky, Here Comes The Thumb.
content.clinical: A fall on an outstretched hand can break the scaphoid, a small wrist bone. Pain in the hollow at the base of the thumb is a key warning sign.
content.hint: Find the small wrist bones and palm bones just past the lower ends of the forearm bones.
